history.q: Which son of Erik the Red led a Norse voyage to North America around 1000 CE?
history.fact: Leif called the land he found Vinland; Norse ruins at L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland confirm a Viking presence there around 1000 CE.

history.q: From which country did most of Iceland's Viking-Age settlers sail?
history.fact: Many settlers also brought wives and enslaved people from Ireland and Scotland, and DNA studies show a strong Celtic strand in Iceland's early population.

history.q: Iceland became a fully independent republic in which year?
history.fact: The republic was proclaimed on 17 June 1944 at Þingvellir, the birthday of independence hero Jón Sigurðsson, which is now Iceland's National Day.

history.q: Before becoming a republic, Iceland shared its monarch with which country?
history.fact: Iceland passed under the Danish crown in the late 14th century, when the Norwegian and Danish thrones were united.

history.q: Which country's forces occupied neutral Iceland in May 1940, during the Second World War?
history.fact: British troops landed on 10 May 1940 to keep Iceland out of German hands; United States forces took over its defence the following year.

history.q: The 'Cod Wars' of the 1950s-70s were fishing disputes between Iceland and which country?
history.fact: Icelandic coastguard vessels used net-cutters to sever British trawlers' nets; Iceland won recognition of its 200-nautical-mile fishing zone in 1976.

history.q: Which world chess championship match was held in Reykjavík in 1972?
history.fact: Fischer won the 'Match of the Century'. He later became an Icelandic citizen and is buried in a churchyard near Selfoss.

history.q: Which two leaders met at Höfði House in Reykjavík for a famous 1986 summit?
choices: George H. W. Bush and Boris Yeltsin
John F. Kennedy and Nikita Khrushchev
history.fact: The talks came close to a deal on scrapping nuclear weapons and paved the way for the INF Treaty signed the following year.

history.q: Which Norse explorer, outlawed from Iceland, founded the first Norse settlements in Greenland around 985?
history.fact: The sagas say Erik chose the name 'Greenland' because people would be more eager to go there if it had an attractive name.

history.q: Who is traditionally honoured as Iceland's first permanent Norse settler?
history.fact: Legend says Ingólfur threw his high-seat pillars overboard and settled where they washed ashore: the bay he named Reykjavík.

history.q: In about which year did the Althing accept Christianity as Iceland's official religion?
history.fact: As a compromise, people could still eat horse meat and worship the old gods in private for a time after the conversion.

history.q: Under the 'Old Covenant' of 1262-64, Icelandic chieftains swore allegiance to the king of which country?
history.fact: The agreement ended the Icelandic Commonwealth after decades of violent feuding between powerful chieftain families.

history.q: The 1783-84 eruption of which volcanic fissure caused the famine known as the 'Mist Hardships'?
history.fact: Poisonous gases killed much of Iceland's livestock, and roughly a fifth of the population died; the haze was felt across Europe.

history.q: Which 19th-century scholar led Iceland's campaign for self-rule and gave his birthday to its National Day?
history.fact: Jón Sigurðsson's portrait appears on the 500-krónur note, and his statue faces the Althing building in Reykjavík.

history.q: According to the medieval 'Book of Settlements', which Norse sailor gave Iceland its name after seeing a fjord full of drift ice?
history.fact: He is nicknamed Hrafna-Flóki ('Raven-Flóki') because he released ravens from his ship to lead him to land.

history.q: Norse settlement of Iceland is traditionally dated to which year?
history.fact: Archaeologists have found a layer of volcanic ash from about 871 that lies just beneath the earliest traces of settlement.

history.q: Which country's military operated an air base at Keflavík until 2006?
history.fact: Naval Air Station Keflavik was a Cold War outpost for watching the North Atlantic; the old base area, Ásbrú, now holds homes, schools and startups.

history.q: Where was the Republic of Iceland proclaimed on 17 June 1944?
history.fact: Thousands gathered in pouring rain at the ancient assembly site to see Sveinn Björnsson elected as the first president.

history.q: Which lawspeaker decided in favour of Christianity at the Althing after lying under a cloak for a day and a night?
history.fact: Þorgeir was himself a pagan priest-chieftain; legend says he later threw his idols into the waterfall now called Goðafoss.

history.q: What name is given to the violent 13th-century era of feuds between Iceland's chieftain clans?
history.fact: The era takes its name from the powerful Sturlung family, to which the writer Snorri Sturluson belonged.

history.q: Which Catholic bishop was beheaded at Skálholt in 1550, ending resistance to the Lutheran Reformation in Iceland?
history.fact: Jón Arason, bishop of Hólar, was executed together with two of his sons; he also brought Iceland's first printing press.

history.q: Which island group off Iceland's south coast suffered the worst of the 1627 Barbary pirate raids?
history.fact: Hundreds of Icelanders were taken to Algiers; one captive, Guðríður Símonardóttir, was ransomed and married the poet Hallgrímur Pétursson.

history.q: According to Ari the Wise, which people were already in Iceland when the Norse arrived, but soon left?
history.fact: Ari wrote that the papar left behind Irish books, bells and croziers; place names such as Papey still recall them.

history.q: Which Danish king visited Iceland in 1874 and gave it its first constitution during the millennium of settlement?
history.fact: He was the first reigning monarch to visit Iceland. The national anthem, 'Lofsöngur', was written for the same celebrations.

history.q: In 1397 Iceland, as a Norwegian dependency, became part of which union of Scandinavian crowns?
history.fact: The Kalmar Union joined Denmark, Norway and Sweden under one monarch; Iceland stayed under the Danish crown long after Sweden left.

technology.q: Nearly all of Iceland's electricity comes from which two sources?
technology.fact: Glacial rivers drive the hydro plants and volcanic heat drives the geothermal ones, so Iceland's power supply is almost entirely renewable.

technology.q: Roughly what share of Iceland's homes are heated with geothermal energy?
technology.fact: Hot water piped from boreholes heats homes, greenhouses and even some pavements and car parks in Reykjavík, keeping them free of ice.

technology.q: Which milky-blue geothermal spa near Grindavík is fed by water from the Svartsengi power plant?
technology.fact: The lagoon formed from the power plant's runoff in the 1970s; its colour comes from silica in the warm seawater.

technology.q: Iceland straddles the boundary between which two tectonic plates?
technology.fact: The plates pull apart by about 2 cm a year; at Silfra in Þingvellir divers can swim in a crack between the two continents.

technology.q: Iceland's Ring Road, which loops around the whole island, is numbered as which route?
technology.fact: Completed in 1974, the road runs about 1,300 km and passes many of the island's most famous waterfalls and glaciers.

technology.q: Geothermal water heats which public facility found in almost every Icelandic town?
technology.fact: Swimming lessons are compulsory in Icelandic schools, and the local hot pot is a favourite place to chat with neighbours.

technology.q: Which form of public transport does Iceland not have?
technology.fact: Small, sparse populations and rugged terrain meant no public railway was ever built; travellers go by road, sea or air.

technology.q: Which dark volcanic rock makes up most of Iceland's bedrock?
technology.fact: Cooling basalt lava can crack into the hexagonal columns seen at Reynisfjara beach and Svartifoss waterfall.

technology.q: Ash from Iceland's Eyjafjallajökull volcano caused what major disruption in April 2010?
choices: Air travel across Europe was grounded
North Sea oil platforms were evacuated
technology.fact: More than 100,000 flights were cancelled over about a week, the largest shutdown of European airspace since the Second World War.

technology.q: Which energy-hungry industry uses the largest share of Iceland's electricity?
technology.fact: Cheap renewable power drew aluminium producers to Iceland, which imports bauxite-derived alumina and exports the finished metal.

technology.q: Which massively multiplayer space game is developed by Reykjavík's CCP Games?
technology.fact: Launched in 2003, EVE Online runs on a single shared universe where players have staged battles involving thousands of ships.

technology.q: Which Reykjavík company, founded by Kári Stefánsson in 1996, studies the genetics of the Icelandic population?
technology.fact: deCODE helped create an online genealogy, Íslendingabók, that traces how most Icelanders are related to one another.

technology.q: At the Hellisheiði power plant, the Carbfix project stores carbon dioxide by doing what?
choices: Turning it into stone in basalt rock
Pumping it into old oil wells
Dissolving it in the open sea
technology.fact: CO2 dissolved in water is injected into basalt, where it reacts to form carbonate minerals, mostly within two years.

technology.q: In 1973, how did Icelanders slow the lava flow that threatened the harbour on Heimaey?
choices: By flooding it with river water
technology.fact: Pumps sprayed millions of tonnes of seawater onto the advancing lava from Eldfell, helping to save the vital fishing harbour.

technology.q: What is Iceland's largest geothermal power plant, on the Hengill volcanic system near Reykjavík?
technology.fact: Hellisheiði produces both electricity and hot water, which is piped to homes in the capital area.

technology.q: What is the Icelandic-origin term for a sudden flood when a volcano melts the glacier above it?
technology.fact: Jökulhlaup means 'glacier run'. The 1996 Gjálp eruption under Vatnajökull unleashed one that swept away parts of the Ring Road.

technology.q: The Hvalfjörður Tunnel, opened in 1998 north of Reykjavík, runs where?
choices: Under the seabed of a fjord
technology.fact: About 5.8 km long and reaching 165 m below sea level, it saves drivers a long detour around the fjord.

technology.q: Geothermal greenhouses at Hveragerði have even grown which tropical fruit?
technology.fact: Icelandic greenhouses mostly grow tomatoes, cucumbers and peppers, but a research greenhouse has kept banana plants for decades.

technology.q: Which Icelandic company sells the 'Flex-Foot Cheetah' carbon-fibre running blade?
technology.fact: Founded in Reykjavík in 1971, Össur grew into one of the world's leading makers of prosthetic limbs and orthopaedic braces.

technology.q: Which hydropower project in Iceland's eastern highlands, completed in 2007, feeds the country's largest power station?
technology.fact: Its dams supply the Fljótsdalur station, which powers an aluminium smelter at Reyðarfjörður; the project was hotly debated.

technology.q: In 2009 the Iceland Deep Drilling Project unexpectedly drilled into magma at which volcano?
technology.fact: The drill hit molten rock about 2 km down; the superheated steam it produced was among the hottest ever harnessed from a well.

technology.q: Which bridge, completing Iceland's Ring Road in 1974, was partly swept away by a glacial flood in 1996?
technology.fact: Twisted girders from the damaged bridge are displayed beside the road near Skaftafell as a monument to the flood's power.

technology.q: Iceland's first submarine telegraph cable, laid in 1906, came ashore at which eastern fjord town?
technology.fact: The cable linked Iceland to Europe via the Faroe Islands and Shetland, making Seyðisfjörður a communications hub.

technology.q: Iceland's first hydroelectric power plant was built in 1904 in which town?
technology.fact: Carpenter Jóhannes Reykdal dammed a stream to power his workshop and supply electric light to a handful of homes.

technology.q: Marel, founded in Iceland in 1983, makes machinery for which industry?
technology.fact: Marel began by making electronic scales for fishing boats and grew into a global supplier of fish, meat and poultry processing equipment.

art.q: What are the medieval Icelandic prose stories about early settlers, feuds and heroes called?
art.fact: The Sagas of Icelanders were written down mostly in the 13th and 14th centuries, often by authors whose names are unknown.

art.q: Which Icelandic singer, formerly of The Sugarcubes, released the solo album 'Debut' in 1993?
art.fact: Björk released her first album at the age of 11 and later won Cannes' best actress award for 'Dancer in the Dark'.

art.q: Which Reykjavík church, whose stepped tower evokes basalt columns, is the city's best-known landmark?
art.fact: Designed by Guðjón Samúelsson, it took about 41 years to build, from 1945 to 1986; its tower is about 74 m tall.

art.q: Which Icelandic writer won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1955?
art.fact: His best-known novel, 'Independent People', follows a stubborn sheep farmer's struggle for independence.

art.q: Which Icelandic band scored a worldwide hit with 'Little Talks' in 2011-12?
art.fact: The band formed in 2010 and won Iceland's Músíktilraunir battle of the bands that year before their song spread across the world.

art.q: What covers the roofs and walls of Iceland's traditional farmhouses, such as those at Glaumbær?
art.fact: Timber was scarce, so Icelanders built with turf and stone, which insulated well against the cold for over a thousand years.

art.q: What do Icelanders traditionally give each other on Christmas Eve, a custom behind the 'Jólabókaflóð'?
art.fact: Jólabókaflóð means 'Christmas book flood'; many new books are published in autumn and read late into Christmas Eve.

art.q: Which HBO series filmed many of its icy 'Beyond the Wall' scenes in Iceland?
art.fact: Locations included Lake Mývatn, the glaciers of the south and the Þingvellir rift valley.

art.q: Which Icelandic band is famous for the album 'Ágætis byrjun' and a made-up singing language called 'Hopelandic'?
art.fact: Singer Jónsi often plays his electric guitar with a cello bow, giving the band its soaring, glacial sound.

art.q: What is the name of Reykjavík's glass-fronted harbourside concert hall, opened in 2011?
art.fact: Its facade, made with artist Olafur Eliasson, uses geometric glass blocks; the building won the EU's Mies van der Rohe Award in 2013.

art.q: Who wrote the 'Prose Edda', a key source for Norse mythology, in the 13th century?
art.fact: Much of what we know about Odin, Thor and Loki comes from Snorri's handbook for poets.

art.q: Which Icelandic composer won a Golden Globe for scoring 'The Theory of Everything'?
art.fact: Jóhann Jóhannsson was also Oscar-nominated for 'Sicario'; he died in 2018 aged 48.

art.q: Which saga, often called the greatest of all, ends with a wise lawyer burned in his farmhouse with his family?
art.fact: Njáls saga is set in south Iceland around the year 1000, and fans still visit its farms and battle sites.

art.q: The medieval manuscript Codex Regius preserves which collection of Old Norse poems?
art.fact: Kept in Copenhagen for centuries, it was returned to Iceland in 1971 and greeted by a huge crowd at Reykjavík harbour.

art.q: Which Icelandic crime writer created Inspector Erlendur, hero of 'Jar City'?
art.fact: Arnaldur's novels helped launch the 'Nordic noir' boom; Icelanders read more books per person than most nations.

art.q: Which Danish-Icelandic artist created 'The Weather Project', a giant artificial sun, at Tate Modern in 2003?
art.fact: Eliasson spent childhood summers in Iceland, and its light, ice and landscapes often inspire his work.

art.q: Which 17th-century poet wrote the 'Passion Hymns' and gave his name to Reykjavík's largest church?
art.fact: His 50 Passion Hymns are read aloud on Icelandic radio every year during Lent.

art.q: Icelandic Language Day, 16 November, is the birthday of which Romantic poet?
art.fact: Jónas coined many new Icelandic words, including terms for astronomy, so the language would not need to borrow foreign ones.

art.q: Which Icelandic director made 'Everest' (2015) and created the TV series 'Trapped'?
art.fact: 'Trapped' (Ófærð), about a murder in a snowbound fjord town, became one of Iceland's most successful TV exports.

art.q: Which saga hero, a Viking warrior and poet, is said to have composed his first verse at the age of three?
art.fact: Egill's poem 'Sonatorrek', a lament for his drowned son, is one of the most moving works of Old Norse poetry.

art.q: Which outlaw saga hero spent his last years hiding on the cliff-bound island of Drangey?
art.fact: Grettir was said to be Iceland's longest-surviving outlaw; a hot pool near Drangey, Grettislaug, is named after him.

art.q: Which Icelandic artist made 'The Visitors' (2012), a nine-screen musical video filmed in a farmhouse in New York State?
art.fact: Each musician was filmed alone in a different room of the old house, all playing the same song together for over an hour.

art.q: Which landscape painter, known for mossy lava scenes, appears on Iceland's 2,000-krónur banknote?
art.fact: Kjarvalsstaðir, part of Reykjavík Art Museum, is named after him and holds a large collection of his work.

art.q: Who wrote the words of Iceland's national anthem, 'Lofsöngur'?
art.fact: Written for the 1874 millennium celebrations, with music by Sveinbjörn Sveinbjörnsson, it is notoriously hard to sing.

art.q: Which 2018 Icelandic film follows a choir conductor who secretly sabotages the power lines of an aluminium smelter?
art.fact: Directed by Benedikt Erlingsson, the film features a live band and choir that appear on screen to play its soundtrack.

politics.q: What is the name of Iceland's parliament?
politics.fact: Founded in 930, the Althing is often called one of the world's oldest surviving parliaments.

politics.q: In 1980, Vigdís Finnbogadóttir became the world's first democratically elected female what?
politics.fact: A single mother and former theatre director, Vigdís served four terms, from 1980 to 1996.

politics.q: Iceland is a founding member of NATO, but it has no what?
politics.fact: Iceland joined NATO in 1949; its Coast Guard and allied air patrols handle much of its defence.

politics.q: Which of these organisations is Iceland NOT a member of?
politics.fact: Iceland applied to join the EU in 2009 but halted talks in 2013; it trades with the EU through the European Economic Area.

politics.q: Where did the Althing hold its open-air assemblies from 930 until the late 18th century?
politics.fact: Þingvellir, 'the assembly plains', sits in a rift valley between two tectonic plates and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

politics.q: In 2009, who became Iceland's first female prime minister and the world's first openly gay head of government?
politics.fact: When same-sex marriage became legal in Iceland in 2010, Jóhanna married her long-time partner, the writer Jónína Leósdóttir.

politics.q: On 24 October 1975, about 90% of Icelandic women did what to show their importance to society?
choices: Took the day off work and housework
politics.fact: Schools, shops and phone lines struggled, fathers took children to work, and five years later Iceland elected a woman president.

politics.q: Which Icelandic prime minister resigned in April 2016 after the Panama Papers revelations?
politics.fact: Leaked papers linked his family to an offshore company, and thousands of protesters gathered outside the Althing.

politics.q: Which comedian became mayor of Reykjavík in 2010 after founding the satirical 'Best Party'?
politics.fact: His jokey campaign promises included free towels at swimming pools and a polar bear for the city zoo.

politics.q: Who served as Iceland's president for five terms, from 1996 to 2016?
politics.fact: He was the first president to use the veto, and he sent two Icesave repayment deals to referendums in 2010 and 2011.

politics.q: Iceland's 2011 draft constitution was notable for what?
choices: Being drafted entirely by foreign experts
Inviting public suggestions online and on social media
politics.fact: Voters backed it as a basis for a new constitution in a 2012 advisory referendum, but the Althing never adopted it.

politics.q: What is the name of the official residence of Iceland's president, near Reykjavík?
politics.fact: Bessastaðir was once the seat of Danish royal officials, and the farm was home to the medieval chieftain Snorri Sturluson for a time.

politics.q: In 2018 Iceland became the first country to require large employers to prove what?
choices: That they pay women and men equally
That they employ no foreign workers
That they offer a four-day week
politics.fact: Firms with 25 or more staff must obtain official equal-pay certification or face fines.

politics.q: Which Icelandic party was formed in 1929 by a merger of the Conservative and Liberal parties?
politics.fact: The centre-right party was Iceland's largest for most of the 20th century and has often led coalition governments.

politics.q: In 1975 Iceland extended its exclusive fishing zone to how many nautical miles?
politics.fact: The move sparked the third and final Cod War with Britain, which ended in 1976 with Iceland's limit accepted.

politics.q: At the medieval Althing, what was the lawspeaker's chief duty at the Law Rock?
politics.fact: Before the laws were written down, the lawspeaker recited a third of them aloud each summer, covering them all over three years.

politics.q: What status did Iceland gain on 1 December 1918?
choices: A sovereign kingdom sharing Denmark's king
politics.fact: Under the Act of Union, Denmark still handled Iceland's foreign affairs, but either side could end the union after 25 years.

politics.q: Protests that helped topple Iceland's government in January 2009 are nicknamed after which household items?
politics.fact: Crowds outside the Althing banged kitchenware for weeks after the bank collapse; Prime Minister Geir Haarde's government resigned.

politics.q: How many members sit in Iceland's Althing?
politics.fact: The 63 members are elected by proportional representation from six constituencies for terms of up to four years.

politics.q: Who was elected the first president of Iceland in 1944?
politics.fact: Sveinn Björnsson had served as regent of Iceland since 1941, after contact with the Danish king was cut by the war.

politics.q: Which former prime minister was tried by the special Landsdómur court over the 2008 banking collapse?
politics.fact: The court convened for the first time ever and in 2012 convicted him on one minor charge, imposing no punishment.

politics.q: Who served as Iceland's prime minister from 1991 to 2004, the longest continuous term?
politics.fact: Before leading the government, Davíð Oddsson was mayor of Reykjavík; he later became a central bank governor and newspaper editor.

politics.q: Which Icelandic party, traditionally strongest among farmers and rural voters, was founded in 1916?
politics.fact: The Progressive Party is Iceland's oldest existing political party and has frequently been part of coalition governments.

politics.q: In 2010 and 2011 Icelanders voted in referendums to reject deals to repay foreign depositors of which online bank scheme?
politics.fact: Icesave belonged to the failed Landsbanki; in 2013 the EFTA Court ruled that Iceland had not breached its obligations.

politics.q: After being abolished in 1800, the Althing was revived as an advisory assembly in Reykjavík in which decade?
politics.fact: Re-established by royal decree in 1843, it first met in 1845 and gained law-making powers with the 1874 constitution.

current-affairs.q: In March 2021, a volcanic eruption began at which mountain on the Reykjanes Peninsula, the area's first in nearly 800 years?
current-affairs.fact: The easy-to-reach eruption drew hundreds of thousands of visitors, who hiked out to watch lava fountains in the Geldingadalir valley.

current-affairs.q: In November 2023, which fishing town on the Reykjanes Peninsula was evacuated as magma surged beneath it?
current-affairs.fact: About 3,700 residents left on 10 November 2023; in January 2024 lava reached the town's edge and destroyed several houses.

current-affairs.q: Who was elected President of Iceland in June 2024?
current-affairs.fact: A businesswoman who had also run in 2016, Halla Tómasdóttir took office on 1 August 2024 as Iceland's second woman president.

current-affairs.q: In 2020 Icelandic composer Hildur Guðnadóttir won the Oscar for Best Original Score for which film?
current-affairs.fact: She also won a Golden Globe, a BAFTA and a Grammy for 'Joker', and an Emmy for the TV series 'Chernobyl'.

current-affairs.q: Which Icelandic singer won a Grammy in February 2024 for her album 'Bewitched'?
current-affairs.fact: Laufey's jazz-inspired songs won Best Traditional Pop Vocal Album; she is a trained classical cellist.

current-affairs.q: Daði Freyr's viral song 'Think About Things' was Iceland's entry for which 2020 contest, cancelled because of COVID-19?
current-affairs.fact: The song's dance routine and knitted green jumpers spread worldwide online even though the contest never took place.

current-affairs.q: Which Icelandic low-cost airline collapsed in March 2019, stranding thousands of passengers?
current-affairs.fact: WOW air's bright purple planes had offered cheap transatlantic fares with stopovers in Iceland.

current-affairs.q: Who became Iceland's prime minister in December 2024, the youngest in the country's history?
current-affairs.fact: Aged 36, the Social Democratic Alliance leader formed a coalition of three parties, all of them led by women.

current-affairs.q: In August 2019, Icelanders held a memorial for which glacier, the first in the country lost to climate change?
current-affairs.fact: A plaque titled 'A letter to the future', written by author Andri Snær Magnason, now marks the spot.

current-affairs.q: Which Icelandic prime minister resigned in April 2024 to run for president?
current-affairs.fact: Katrín had led the government since 2017; she finished second in the June 2024 presidential election.

current-affairs.q: Which party won the most seats in Iceland's November 2024 snap election?
current-affairs.fact: The Left-Green Movement, which had led the previous government, lost all of its seats.

current-affairs.q: In 2021, which Swiss company opened 'Orca', then the world's largest plant capturing CO2 directly from the air, in Iceland?
current-affairs.fact: Orca was designed to remove up to 4,000 tonnes of CO2 a year, which Carbfix then stores as rock underground.

current-affairs.q: On 24 October 2023, Prime Minister Katrín Jakobsdóttir joined what nationwide action?
choices: A women's strike against unequal pay and gender-based violence
A general strike of fishing crews
current-affairs.fact: It was the first full-day women's strike in Iceland since the famous 'Women's Day Off' of 1975.

current-affairs.q: In June 2023, Iceland temporarily suspended which activity on animal-welfare grounds?
current-affairs.fact: A government report found that killing the whales took too long; hunting resumed that September under stricter rules.

current-affairs.q: During the Reykjanes eruptions of 2023-24, what did Icelanders build to shield the Svartsengi power plant from lava?
current-affairs.fact: Bulldozers piled up long walls of rock and soil that diverted lava flows away from the plant and the Blue Lagoon.

current-affairs.q: In May 2023, Reykjavík hosted only the fourth-ever summit of which organisation's leaders?
current-affairs.fact: The summit set up a register to record damage caused by the war in Ukraine.

current-affairs.q: A widely reported 2021 analysis of Icelandic trials held from 2015 to 2019 found success with what workplace change?
choices: A shorter working week without a pay cut
current-affairs.fact: Workers' wellbeing improved while productivity held steady, and unions went on to win shorter hours for most of the workforce.

current-affairs.q: In 2023, OpenAI said Iceland's government had worked with it to improve GPT-4's handling of what?
current-affairs.fact: Iceland sees AI as a way to keep its small language thriving in a digital world dominated by English.

current-affairs.q: In 2021, Daði og Gagnamagnið finished in which place at the Eurovision Song Contest with '10 Years'?
current-affairs.fact: After a band member tested positive for COVID-19, the act competed using a recording of their rehearsal.

current-affairs.q: In August 2022, a new eruption began in which valley near Fagradalsfjall?
current-affairs.fact: It was the second eruption in the area in two years, followed by another at nearby Litli-Hrútur in July 2023.

current-affairs.q: From December 2023, a string of eruptions broke out along which crater row just north of Grindavík?
current-affairs.fact: The crater row erupted again and again over the following months, each time after magma refilled a chamber beneath Svartsengi.

current-affairs.q: From 2021, Icelandic law extended paid parental leave to how many months in total?
current-affairs.fact: Each parent gets six months, of which six weeks can be transferred to the other parent.

current-affairs.q: Who succeeded Katrín Jakobsdóttir as Iceland's prime minister in April 2024?
current-affairs.fact: It was Bjarni's second spell as prime minister, after a short term in 2017; his coalition collapsed that October.

current-affairs.q: In January 2024, which Icelandic president announced he would not seek a third term?
current-affairs.fact: A historian before entering office in 2016, Guðni made the announcement in his New Year's Day address.

current-affairs.q: In early 2020, ground uplift at which mountain near Grindavík first signalled renewed volcanic unrest on Reykjanes?
current-affairs.fact: Swarms of earthquakes and a few centimetres of uplift prompted a warning; eruptions followed on the peninsula from 2021.

general.q: Which is the world's northernmost capital of a sovereign state?
general.fact: Reykjavík lies at about 64° north; around midsummer the sun barely sets, while in midwinter there are only about four hours of daylight.

general.q: The English word 'geyser' comes from the name of a hot spring in which country?
general.fact: Geysir in Haukadalur is now mostly quiet, but its neighbour Strokkur shoots water about 20 m into the air every few minutes.

general.q: Which small, sturdy breed with an extra smooth gait called the tölt is native to Iceland?
general.fact: Horses may not be imported into Iceland, and an Icelandic horse that leaves the country can never return.

general.q: Which seabird with a colourful striped beak nests in huge numbers on Iceland's cliffs each summer?
general.fact: Iceland hosts the world's largest puffin population; in the Westman Islands children help lost pufflings find their way to sea.

general.q: At Euro 2016, Iceland famously knocked which team out of the round of 16?
general.fact: Iceland won 2-1 in Nice, and its fans' thunderous 'Viking clap' became famous around the world.

general.q: How are most Icelanders' last names formed?
choices: From the name of the family farm
From a parent's first name plus -son or -dóttir
From a clan name passed down for centuries
general.fact: Because surnames change every generation, Icelanders address each other by first name, and the phone book is sorted that way too.

general.q: What is Iceland's largest glacier?
general.fact: Vatnajökull covers about 8% of Iceland and hides several active volcanoes, including Grímsvötn, beneath its ice.

general.q: What is skyr, eaten in Iceland for over a thousand years?
general.fact: Skyr is technically a soft cheese, though it is eaten like a thick, protein-rich yoghurt, often with berries.

general.q: Reykjavík's name, meaning 'Smoky Bay', was inspired by what?
general.fact: The settler Ingólfur Arnarson is said to have named the bay after the plumes of steam he saw rising from the ground.

general.q: Modern Icelandic is famously close to which medieval language, letting readers enjoy the sagas in the original?
general.fact: Instead of borrowing foreign words, Icelanders coin new ones: a computer is a 'tölva', blending the words for number and prophetess.

general.q: What is the Icelandic delicacy hákarl?
general.fact: Greenland shark meat is toxic when fresh, so it is fermented and hung to dry for months; its ammonia smell is legendary.

general.q: How many Yule Lads visit Icelandic children in the days before Christmas?
general.fact: Arriving one by one from 12 December, these mischievous sons of the troll Grýla leave gifts in shoes placed on windowsills.

general.q: Which black-sand beach near Vík is famous for its basalt columns and dangerous 'sneaker waves'?
general.fact: Offshore stand the Reynisdrangar sea stacks, which legend says are trolls caught by the sunrise and turned to stone.

general.q: Which glacier lagoon, filled with drifting icebergs, lies beside the Ring Road in southeast Iceland?
general.fact: Ice chunks washed onto the nearby black-sand shore sparkle like gems, giving it the nickname Diamond Beach.

general.q: Which waterfall in southern Iceland has a path that lets visitors walk behind its curtain of water?
general.fact: The water drops about 60 m over a former sea cliff that dates from when the coastline lay further inland.

general.q: What was the only land mammal living in Iceland before humans arrived?
general.fact: Arctic foxes probably walked over sea ice during the last ice age. Reindeer and mink were introduced by people much later.

general.q: Which Icelandic volcano was known in medieval Europe as a gateway to hell?
general.fact: Hekla is one of Iceland's most active volcanoes and has erupted more than 20 times since the settlement era.

general.q: In which Jules Verne novel do explorers descend into the crater of Iceland's Snæfellsjökull?
choices: Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Seas
Journey to the Centre of the Earth
Around the World in Eighty Days
general.fact: Verne's heroes follow a coded message from an Icelandic alchemist and finally emerge from the volcano Stromboli in Italy.

general.q: Which waterfall, linked to Iceland's conversion to Christianity, is called the 'waterfall of the gods'?
general.fact: Legend says the lawspeaker Þorgeir threw his statues of the old Norse gods into its waters after the conversion.

general.q: Which island, crossed by the Arctic Circle, is Iceland's northernmost inhabited place?
general.fact: The Arctic Circle shifts over time, so a giant concrete sphere marking it on Grímsey is moved to follow the line.

general.q: Which lake in north Iceland is named after the swarms of insects that hatch there?
general.fact: Mývatn means 'midge lake'. The midges feed huge numbers of ducks, making it one of Europe's best birdwatching spots.

general.q: What is Iceland's highest peak?
general.fact: Rising about 2,110 m, it sits on the crater rim of Öræfajökull, an ice-covered volcano at the southern edge of Vatnajökull.

general.q: Which form of wrestling is Iceland's traditional national sport?
general.fact: Wrestlers wear leather belts around the waist and thighs and must stay upright while trying to trip their opponent.

general.q: Which volcanic island rose from the sea off Iceland's south coast in an eruption beginning in 1963?
general.fact: Only scientists may land on Surtsey, a UNESCO site where they study how plants and animals colonise new land.

general.q: Which waterfall in northeast Iceland is often called the most powerful in Europe?
general.fact: Fed by meltwater from Vatnajökull, it plunges about 45 m into the Jökulsárgljúfur canyon.
